processing: Fresh leaf is heated to stop enzymes, rolled, fermented without air, pounded, shaped and dried. Food-grade tea ferments about two months and stays moist, while drinking tea ferments four to nine months and is sun-dried.
harvest_season: Little is recorded about a prized picking; what defines the tea is the length of fermentation.
appearance_dry: Drinking grades are dried, pressed pieces or slices; food grades remain moist.
appearance_liquor: No reliable colour record exists; a pale golden tone is a rough expectation only.
appearance_wet: Pounded, broken leaf rather than whole leaves, as the pounding step implies.
taste_profile: Sour by name and by its lactic fermentation; precise tasting notes are scarce, so expect tartness rather than any fixed flavour.

brewing.notes: For the dried drinking kind only; general guidance, not a local rule. The moist kind is cooked as food with other ingredients.

vintage_note: Sold by type rather than by vintage: moist tea for eating after about two months of fermentation, or dried tea for drinking after four to nine months. Little is recorded about aging it further, so buy it fairly fresh from a named Santaishan maker when possible.
description:
De'ang Suan Cha is the sour tea of the De'ang people in Mangshi, Yunnan, centred on Santaishan, China's only De'ang ethnic township. Its fermentation runs without air, unlike the aerobic fermentation of other tea types.

That is the distinct part. Fresh leaf is cooked, rolled and sealed away to ferment, then pounded and shaped. The sealed fermentation encourages lactic acid bacteria, which sets it apart from teas fermented in open air.

There are really two products. The short-fermented moist tea is an ingredient, cooked into dishes. The longer-fermented dried tea is what you brew, and since it has few published tasting notes, go gently: a small amount and short steeps first.

When buying, make sure you know which one you have, as one is food and the other a drink. Village producers around Chudonggua have built a local industry around it.
history:
The craft has passed by word of mouth between teacher and apprentice, so the older record is thin and no founding date can be given. Its recognised modern status is clearer: it entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2021.

In 2022 it was included as part of the UNESCO listing for traditional Chinese tea processing and associated customs. Since then it has also become a rural income source in places such as Chudonggua village, where villagers including Yang Chunlan have led production.
